classification.difficultyReason: Translate the absence of exact change into restrictions on coin counts and mixed subsets, derive a global upper bound, and verify an attaining collection has no subset worth one frac.

content.prompt: In Fracland the basic unit of currency is called a frac, for which they have a one-frac note. Smaller denominations are coins. They have half-frac, third-frac, quarter-frac and fifth-frac coins. What is the largest sum of money you could carry without having exact change for a one-frac note?

spec.sourceRegion: Left column, four coins beneath question 19
spec.description: Four unfilled circular coins in a horizontal row, preserving denomination order and F labels. Decorative textures and colours are omitted.
spec.mathematics: Left to right: 1/5 F, 1/4 F, 1/3 F, 1/2 F.
spec.answerVisibility: All four denominations are permanent givens.

answer.short:
$\frac{133}{60}$ frac.

One maximum collection has one half-frac, two third-frac, one quarter-frac and four fifth-frac coins.
answer.worked:
There can be at most one half-frac, two third-frac, three quarter-frac and four fifth-frac coins; otherwise coins of one denomination alone make one frac. A one-frac note also cannot be carried.

If there is a half-frac coin, there can be at most one quarter-frac coin, since a half and two quarters make one frac. Thus the total is at most
$$\begin{align*}\frac12+\frac23+\frac14+\frac45&=\frac{30+40+15+48}{60}\\\frac12+\frac23+\frac14+\frac45&=\frac{133}{60}.\end{align*}$$
Without a half-frac coin, the total is at most
$$\frac23+\frac34+\frac45=\frac{133}{60}.$$
The first collection attains this bound. To check that it cannot make one frac, measure values in sixtieths. Any subset making one frac would satisfy $30a+20b+15c+12d=60$, where $0\le a\le1$, $0\le b\le2$, $0\le c\le1$ and $0\le d\le4$. Reduction modulo $5$ forces $d=0$. If $a=0$, the available thirds and quarter total at most $55$ sixtieths. If $a=1$, the remaining $30$ cannot be made from up to two $20$s and one $15$. Hence exact change is impossible, and the maximum is $\frac{133}{60}$ frac.
